..
Issued at 200 PM EDT Mon Aug 10 2026

Pattern / Forecast Synopsis: 

Progressive WNW flow regime to prevail through the rest of the week, 
with northern Michigan lying north of a stationary boundary 
(analyzed from roughly Omaha to Cleveland to Philadelphia) that will 
remain the focus of several convectively charged waves. Result is 
much deeper moisture pooling well to our south, with modest moisture 
remaining overhead... just enough for potential mesoscale 
shenanigans. Disheveled surface high overhead will not exactly 
dissuade the notion of convective development along the Lake Huron 
breeze boundary along with eastern upper the next couple days before 
a weak wave traverses the region, bringing scattered convection 
potential to the entirety of the CWA. 500mb ridge axis builds after 
midweek, with plume of monsoonal moisture coincides with a trough 
building into the Plains. Guidance seems bullish on an associated 
deepening surface low to make a pass at the upper Great Lakes over 
the weekend. On paper, this should be sufficient enough to force the 
aforementioned stationary front northward, and the combination of 
monsoonal origin moisture coupled with return flow drawing Gulf 
moisture northward conceptually should bring a more widespread and 
appreciable rainfall chance across the region Saturday into Sunday. 
Following the passage of this feature, the pattern shifts back into 
progressive NW flow, which should lead to more quick-moving 
convectively charged shortwaves making passes through the Great 
Lakes, though it's a bit far out to pinpoint where exactly any 
convective complexes occur next week. 

Details: 

Today-Tuesday: Ongoing robust convective complexes over Ohio 
showcase the barrier that the aforementioned stationary front 
presents between deeper moisture and the modest moisture overhead. 
Most of the convection that has wavered north of the front has 
floundered considerably while activity south of the front (in the 
deeper moisture) has been able to maintain itself quite well. As 
such, anticipation is that convective responses will remain muted 
overhead. Lack of overall synoptic forcing will leave coverage to an 
isolated footprint today, limited to the Lake Huron lake breeze 
area. Limited shear and instability will suppress severe potential. 
Somewhat deeper moisture builds Tuesday, Light west to southwest 
flow will maximize lake breeze convergence across northeast lower 
and eastern upper, and thus, that will be where greatest storm 
potential lies. Scattered downpours will be possible, but not 
looking like a washout by any means. 

Wednesday-Friday: Embedded shortwave passage coupled with continued 
deeper moisture will drum up a much more widespread footprint of 
shower and storm potential Wednesday. Timing of this feature might 
actually be halfway decent to overlap "greatest" synoptic forcing 
with peak heating, thus leading to the more "widespread" footprint 
of convection that includes northwest lower too. Severe potential 
looks limited Wednesday too, with downpours likely posing the 
greatest hazard at this juncture. In the wake of this system, area 
of Canadian surface high pressure intrudes from the northwest in 
conjunction with a 500mb ridge axis, delivering a drier airmass to 
the region (and perhaps a brief reprieve from the thick blanket of 
Pacific NW wildfire smoke aloft). Temperatures trend near to below 
normal Thursday and Friday (highs in the 70s), with cooler nights 
(lows in the 40s and 50s likely). 

Weekend-Next Week: Ridge overhead breaks down as SWerly flow brings 
the next disturbance to the region. Guidance is all over the place 
in regard to the evolution of this wave, and will likely be dictated 
by convective evolution over the Plains. Bottom line- this system 
looks to build a relatively deep moisture plume into the region, 
which should support heavy rainfall potential. As is always the case 
in this delightful little slice of planet earth, every little 
intricate detail has to be perfect for us to get widespread heavier 
rain with moderate to weak synoptic support. I'm convinced something 
as simple as a fly getting swatted by a horse's tail in Manton can 
lead to a series of ludicrous domino effects that entirely derail a 
convection / thunderstorm setup in northern Michigan, though I 
should disclose that I have also been accused of being entirely too 
pessimistic in this regard. Nonetheless, still a lot of detail to 
unpack on this upcoming system, but the potential is there for 
appreciable rainfall on a bit more widespread scale than what we 
have seen the last couple weeks. If the timing is primed in regard 
to our field of instability, perhaps even a severe storm element can 
materialize. Following the passage of this system into next week, NW 
flow returns, which, conceptually supports more rounds of rain and 
thunder via convective complexes building upstream.
